## Project Proposal/Statistical Analysis Plan

Link to your team's Github Repo:

<https://github.com/parvxi/ids702-team-project>

### Dataset Option 1

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Project Title: Cooling Demand, Housing Type, and Household Electricity Use in the United States

Data citation (use APA formatting or something similar): U.S. Energy Information Administration. (2024). *2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) public use microdata file* (Version 7) \[Data set\]. <https://www.eia.gov/consumption/residential/data/2020/index.php?view=microdata>

Original data collection date (when was the dataset published?): Survey reference year 2020. The final microdata file was first published in June 2023; this analysis uses Version 7 of the file, released in January 2024.

Data pull date (when did you download the data you will use?): November 5, 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1 Research Question

**Primary research question:** Among U.S. households, is cooling demand (measured by cooling degree days) associated with annual household electricity use, and does this association differ by housing type (single-family detached, single-family attached, apartment, or mobile home), after adjusting for home size, household size, household income, the age of the home, and main space-heating fuel?

**Backup research question:** Is home size (square footage) associated with annual household electricity use, and does this association differ across climate regions, after adjusting for housing type, household size, and household income?

#### 2 Study Population

The observation unit is a housing unit occupied as a primary residence, together with the household that lives in it. The data come from the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS), a national sample survey conducted by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) that collects energy-related data for housing units occupied as primary residences and the households that live in them. EIA collected data from nearly 18,500 households (18,496 in the public-use file) in housing units statistically selected to represent the 123.5 million housing units occupied as primary residences in the United States. Households reported their housing and household characteristics through the RECS household survey, and the final public-use file also includes EIA's estimates of each household's annual energy consumption and expenditures.

#### 3 Outcomes, Exposures, and Additional Variables of Interest

3.1 Primary Outcome(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `KWH` | Total household electricity use in 2020, in kilowatt-hours, including self-generated solar power (estimated by EIA's end-use model) | Numeric, continuous (range 42 to 184,102 kWh). We plan to analyze log(kWh); the EDA will check the shape of the distribution. |

3.2 Primary Independent Variable(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `CDD65` | Cooling degree days in 2020 (base temperature 65°F), derived from the weighted temperatures of nearby weather stations | Numeric (range 0 to 5,534); rescaled to units of 1,000 cooling degree days for interpretation. |
| `TYPEHUQ` | Type of housing unit (moderator in the cooling degree days × housing type interaction) | Original: 1 = Mobile home, 2 = Single-family house detached, 3 = Single-family house attached (e.g., duplex, row house, townhome), 4 = Apartment in a building with 2 to 4 units, 5 = Apartment in a building with 5 or more units. Recoded: Single-family detached (reference), Single-family attached, Apartment (codes 4 and 5 combined), Mobile home. |

3.3 Additional Variables of Interest (including potential confounders)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `TOTSQFT_EN` | Total energy-consuming area of the home in square feet, including main living areas, basements, and heated, cooled, or finished attics and garages (primary independent variable for the backup research question) | Numeric (range 200 to 15,000; rounded to the nearest 10). |
| `NHSLDMEM` | Number of household members | Numeric, 1 to 7 (top-coded at 7). |
| `MONEYPY` | Annual gross household income for the past year | 16 ordered categories (1 = Less than \$5,000, ..., 16 = \$150,000 or more); will be collapsed into fewer income groups. |
| `YEARMADERANGE` | Range of years when the home was built | 1 = Before 1950, 2 = 1950 to 1959, 3 = 1960 to 1969, 4 = 1970 to 1979, 5 = 1980 to 1989, 6 = 1990 to 1999, 7 = 2000 to 2009, 8 = 2010 to 2015, 9 = 2016 to 2020; categorical. |
| `FUELHEAT` | Main space-heating fuel | 1 = Natural gas, 2 = Propane, 3 = Fuel oil, 5 = Electricity, 7 = Wood or pellets, 99 = Other, -2 = Not applicable (no space heating). Recoded: Electricity, Natural gas, Other or none. |
| `BA_climate` | Building America climate zone (moderator for the backup research question) | Categorical with 8 zones: Cold, Hot-Dry, Hot-Humid, Marine, Mixed-Dry, Mixed-Humid, Subarctic, Very-Cold. Sparse zones may be combined after checking counts. |
| `NWEIGHT` | Final analysis weight; the file also includes 60 replicate weights (`NWEIGHT1` to `NWEIGHT60`) | Numeric (range 437.9 to 29,279.1). |

#### 4 Statistical Analysis Plan

4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis

The outcome is continuous and right-skewed, so we will plot histograms of annual electricity use in kWh and of log kWh to decide on the scale for modelling. To preview the interaction, we will plot electricity use (log scale) against cooling degree days with a separate trend line for each housing type, and compare the levels and spread of electricity use across housing types with a boxplot. Finally, a "Table 1" will summarise the potential confounders (floor area, household size, income, year built and heating fuel) by housing type to see how comparable the groups are.

4.2 Statistical Model (write in mathematical notation and define each term)
We will fit a multiple linear regression:

$$
\log(Y_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1 C_i+
\sum_{h=1}^{3}\alpha_h H_{ih}+
\sum_{h=1}^{3}\delta_h(C_iH_{ih})+
\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{T}\mathbf{Z}_i+\epsilon_i.
$$

Here, $Y_i$ is annual electricity use in kWh; $C_i$ is cooling degree days divided by 1,000; and $H_{ih}$ indicates attached houses, apartments, or mobile homes, with detached houses as the reference. The adjustment variables $\mathbf{Z}_i$ are floor area (in thousands of square feet), household size, income group, year-built category, and heating-fuel category, coded as described in section 3. The intercept is $\beta_0$; $\beta_1$ is the cooling-demand slope for detached houses; $\alpha_h$ gives housing-type differences at zero cooling degree days; $\delta_h$ gives differences in slopes; $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ contains adjustment coefficients; and $\epsilon_i$ is the error term. We will test whether all three $\delta_h$ coefficients are zero.

We will use an ordinary, unweighted model. This does not account for the survey sampling design, so results will describe associations in the analyzed sample, with possible limitations to standard errors and population generalizability.

4.2 Rationale for the statistical model (why are you choosing to use this type of model? What about your data structure/characteristics are you accommodating with this model type?)

Electricity use is continuous and right-skewed, while its log is more symmetric in the EDA. We will therefore start with linear regression of log electricity use and check its residuals. The interaction answers whether cooling demand has a different association with electricity use across housing types. The adjustment variables account for other household and housing differences. Because the outcome is logged, associations describe proportional differences rather than absolute kWh differences. Results will not be interpreted as causal effects.

4.3 Model Assumptions

We assume the conditional mean of log electricity use is adequately represented by the model, errors are independent across households, residual variance is reasonably constant, and residuals are approximately normal for conventional inference. We also assume no severe collinearity or observations that dominate the estimates. Cooling degree days should overlap across housing types. The ordinary-model independence assumption may be limited by the survey design.

4.4 Model Assessment (how will you assess the assumptions and model performance?)

We will inspect residual-versus-fitted plots, residual patterns against continuous predictors, and a residual Q–Q plot. We will check variance inflation factors, leverage, and Cook’s distance. We will report adjusted R-squared and residual error on the log scale, coefficient estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values. A partial F-test will compare models with and without the interaction terms. We will plot fitted relationships by housing type and consider transformations or nonlinear terms if diagnostics show problems.

#### Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(gtsummary)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

options(width = 75)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "top"))

housing_cols <- c("Detached house" = "#2a78d6", "Attached house" = "#1baf7a",
                  "Apartment" = "#eb6834", "Mobile home" = "#6b6b6b")

# Tick marks for log-scale kWh axes, close enough together to read values off
kwh_breaks <- c(100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000)
```

```{r}
#| label: recs-data
recs <- read_csv("data/recs2020/recs2020_public_v7.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    household_id        = DOEID,
    electricity_kwh     = KWH,
    cooling_degree_days = CDD65,
    housing_type = case_when(
      TYPEHUQ == 2     ~ "Detached house",      # single-family detached
      TYPEHUQ == 3     ~ "Attached house",      # single-family attached
      TYPEHUQ %in% 4:5 ~ "Apartment",
      TYPEHUQ == 1     ~ "Mobile home"
    ) |> factor(levels = names(housing_cols)),
    floor_area_sqft = TOTSQFT_EN,
    household_size  = NHSLDMEM,
    heating_fuel = case_when(
      FUELHEAT == 5 ~ "Electricity",
      FUELHEAT == 1 ~ "Natural gas",
      TRUE          ~ "Other or none"
    ),
    year_built = factor(YEARMADERANGE, levels = 1:9,
                        labels = c("Before 1950", "1950s", "1960s", "1970s", "1980s",
                                   "1990s", "2000s", "2010-2015", "2016-2020")),
    income_band = cut(MONEYPY, breaks = c(0, 6, 10, 12, 14, 16),
                      labels = c("Under $20k", "$20k to $39k", "$40k to $59k",
                                 "$60k to $99k", "$100k or more"))
  )

# Group sizes and medians quoted in the text
n_type   <- table(recs$housing_type)
med_type <- tapply(recs$electricity_kwh, recs$housing_type, median)

glimpse(recs)
```

The data have `r comma(nrow(recs))` households, one per row. No household is missing the outcome, and the selected variables have `r sum(is.na(recs))` missing values in total. There are `r comma(n_type[["Detached house"]])` detached houses, `r comma(n_type[["Attached house"]])` attached houses, `r comma(n_type[["Apartment"]])` apartments and `r comma(n_type[["Mobile home"]])` mobile homes. All summaries are unweighted.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recs-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Annual household electricity use in 2020, in kWh (left, cut off at 40,000 kWh for readability) and on the log scale (right)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2
p_kwh <- ggplot(recs, aes(electricity_kwh)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1000, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 40000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Annual electricity use (kWh)", y = "Households")

p_log <- ggplot(recs, aes(log(electricity_kwh))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.15, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "log(annual electricity use in kWh)", y = "Households")

p_kwh + p_log
```

Electricity use is right-skewed: the median is `r comma(median(recs$electricity_kwh))` kWh, the mean is `r comma(mean(recs$electricity_kwh))` kWh and the largest value is `r comma(max(recs$electricity_kwh))` kWh. The log is roughly symmetric, so we will model log kWh (@fig-recs-outcome).

```{r}
#| label: fig-recs-interaction
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity use (log scale) against cooling degree days in 2020, by housing type, with a straight trend line for each type. More cooling degree days means a hotter year."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-align: center
#| dev: png
#| dpi: 300
ggplot(recs, aes(cooling_degree_days, electricity_kwh, colour = housing_type)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.2, stroke = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = comma, breaks = kwh_breaks) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = housing_cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Cooling degree days in 2020 (base 65°F)",
       y = "Annual electricity use (kWh, log scale)")
```

Electricity use rises with cooling degree days for every housing type (@fig-recs-interaction). The lines for detached houses and apartments are close to parallel, so on the log scale hot weather raises their use by a similar percentage; the lines for attached houses and mobile homes are somewhat flatter. The interaction may therefore be modest, and the model will test it. Because detached houses start from the highest level, the same percentage means more kWh for them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recs-housing
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity use (log scale) by housing type."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 1.9
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(recs, aes(electricity_kwh, fct_rev(housing_type), fill = housing_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = comma, breaks = kwh_breaks) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = housing_cols) +
  labs(x = "Annual electricity use (kWh, log scale)", y = NULL)
```

Detached houses use about twice as much electricity as apartments (median `r comma(med_type[["Detached house"]])` vs `r comma(med_type[["Apartment"]])` kWh), with attached houses in between (median `r comma(med_type[["Attached house"]])` kWh) (@fig-recs-housing). Mobile homes are a small group that uses about as much as detached houses (median `r comma(med_type[["Mobile home"]])` kWh) despite being much smaller.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-recs-table1
#| tbl-cap: "Household and housing characteristics by housing type, RECS 2020."
recs |>
  select(housing_type, electricity_kwh, cooling_degree_days, floor_area_sqft,
         household_size, heating_fuel, year_built, income_band) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = housing_type,
    type = list(household_size ~ "continuous"),
    digits = list(household_size ~ 0),
    label = list(
      electricity_kwh     ~ "Annual electricity use (kWh)",
      cooling_degree_days ~ "Cooling degree days (base 65°F)",
      floor_area_sqft     ~ "Floor area (square feet)",
      household_size      ~ "Household members",
      heating_fuel        ~ "Main space-heating fuel",
      year_built          ~ "Year built",
      income_band         ~ "Annual household income"
    )
  ) |>
  modify_header(all_stat_cols() ~ "**{level}**") |>   # group sizes are given in the text
  as_gt() |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::px(10))
```

The housing types face similar climates, but they differ on the other variables in our plan (@tbl-recs-table1): detached houses are the largest, have the most people and the highest incomes, apartments and mobile homes more often heat with electricity, and mobile homes are newer. The model will adjust for floor area, household size, income, year built and heating fuel.

### Dataset Option 2

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Project Title: Age, Gender, and Concern About Artificial Intelligence Across 23 Countries

Data citation (use APA formatting or something similar): Pew Research Center. (2026). *Spring 2025 Global Attitudes Survey* \[Data set\]. <https://www.pewresearch.org/dataset/spring-2025-survey-data/>

Original data collection date (when was the dataset published?): Fieldwork was conducted from January 8 to April 26, 2025.

Data pull date (when did you download the data you will use?): November 4, 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1 Research Question

**Primary research question:** Among adults in 23 countries surveyed in 2025, is age associated with being more concerned than excited about the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life, and does this association differ between men and women, after adjusting for education and country?

**Backup research question:** Is awareness of AI (having heard or read a lot, a little, or nothing about it) associated with being more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life, and does this association differ by age group, after adjusting for gender, education, and country?

#### 2 Study Population

The observation unit is an individual adult respondent. The data come from Pew Research Center's Spring 2025 Global Attitudes Survey, a 25-country survey conducted from January 8 to April 26, 2025, under the direction of Gallup, Langer Research Associates, and Social Research Centre. Outside the United States, the survey consists of nationally representative samples totaling 28,333 adults in 24 countries. Interviews were conducted by telephone in Canada, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Poland, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom; face-to-face in Argentina, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Israel, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria, South Africa, and Turkey; and through a mixed-mode, probability-based online panel in Australia. In the United States, Pew asked the questions about awareness of and concern about AI in a separate survey (American Trends Panel Wave 173, June 2025), so the public Spring 2025 dataset covers only the 24 non-U.S. countries. Because the Australian data record age only in broad groups (18–29, 30–49, 50–64, and 65+) rather than in years, our analysis uses the remaining 23 countries, which together include 26,504 respondents before missing responses are excluded.

#### 3 Outcomes, Exposures, and Additional Variables of Interest

3.1 Primary Outcome(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `ai_cncexc` | Q31. "Overall, how would you say the increased use of artificial intelligence in daily life makes you feel?" | Original: 1 = More excited than concerned, 2 = More concerned than excited, 3 = Equally concerned and excited, 8 = Don't know, 9 = Refused. Recoded: 1 = More concerned than excited; 0 = More excited than concerned or equally concerned and excited; 8 and 9 set to missing. |

3.2 Primary Independent Variable(s)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `age` | Q89. "What is your age?" | Numeric, age in years (18 to 97, where 97 = 97 or older); 98 = Don't know and 99 = Refused set to missing. |
| `gender` | Q88. Gender of respondent (moderator in the age × gender interaction) | Original: 1 = Male, 2 = Female. Recoded: 0 = Male (reference), 1 = Female. |

3.3 Additional Variables of Interest (including potential confounders)

| Variable Name | Description | Coding specification |
|----|----|----|
| `country` | Survey country | Categorical with 23 levels (e.g., 2 = Canada, 14 = India, 25 = Mexico); Australia (13) excluded. |
| `d_educ_*` | Q96. Highest level of education completed, asked with country-specific response categories (one variable per country, e.g., `d_educ_canada`, `d_educ_india`) | Country-specific categories (e.g., Canada: 1 = No formal schooling, ..., 11 = Postgraduate or professional degree); 98 = Don't know and 99 = Refused set to missing. Harmonized into one variable, 0 = Lower education, 1 = Higher education, following Pew's ISCED-based approach: in high-income countries, higher = postsecondary or above; in middle-income countries, higher = upper secondary or above. |
| `ai_heard` | Q30. "Have you heard or read a lot, a little, or nothing at all about artificial intelligence?" (primary independent variable for the backup research question) | 1 = A lot, 2 = A little, 3 = Nothing at all; 8 = Don't know and 9 = Refused set to missing. |
| `weight` | General population survey weight provided by Pew | Numeric. Pew's documentation states this weight must be used when analyzing the attitudes and opinions of the general population. |

#### 4 Statistical Analysis Plan

4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis

The outcome is binary, so we will first show the distribution of the original five answers to the AI question with a bar chart and report the share who are more concerned than excited. To preview the interaction, we will plot the share concerned by age group with separate lines for men and women. We will also plot the share concerned by country to see how much country matters, and a "Table 1" will summarise age, AI awareness and country by gender to check how comparable men and women are.

4.2 Statistical Model (write in mathematical notation and define each term)

We will fit a binary logistic regression:

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),\qquad
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)=
\beta_0+\beta_1 A_i+\beta_2 G_i+
\beta_3(A_iG_i)+\beta_4 E_i+
\sum_{c=2}^{23}\gamma_c C_{ic}.
$$

Here, $Y_i=1$ means more concerned than excited about AI, and $Y_i=0$ means either equally concerned and excited or more excited than concerned. $p_i$ is the probability of $Y_i=1$. We will define $A_i=(\text{age}_i-18)/10$, so one unit represents ten years and zero represents age 18. $G_i$ is 1 for women and 0 for men; $E_i$ is 1 for higher education and 0 for lower education using the harmonization in section 3.3. $C_{ic}$ contains country indicators, with Canada as the reference. The intercept is $\beta_0$; $\beta_1$ is the age association for men; $\beta_2$ is the gender difference at age 18; $\beta_3$ is the age × gender interaction; $\beta_4$ is the education association; and $\gamma_c$ represents country differences. We will test $H_0:\beta_3=0$.

Australia will be excluded, as described in section 2. We will exclude missing responses on model variables and report the resulting sample size. The ordinary, unweighted model will describe sample associations rather than population-representative estimates; not accounting for the survey design may affect standard errors and inference.

4.2 Rationale for the statistical model (why are you choosing to use this type of model? What about your data structure/characteristics are you accommodating with this model type?)

The recoded outcome is binary, so logistic regression is appropriate. The age × gender interaction tests whether the association between age and concern differs between men and women. Education and country are included as adjustment variables. Combining equally concerned and more excited responses makes the question focused, but a value of 0 does not mean a respondent has no concern. Country indicators allow baseline concern to differ, while age and gender associations are assumed to be shared across countries.

4.3 Model Assumptions

We assume independent responses, a linear relationship between age and the log odds of concern within each gender, no severe collinearity, and no complete or quasi-complete separation. There should be enough observations in the outcome and predictor categories. Missing-response exclusions may introduce bias, and the ordinary-model independence assumption may be limited by the survey design.

4.4 Model Assessment (how will you assess the assumptions and model performance?)

We will inspect counts across outcome, gender, education, and country categories and check model convergence and unusually large coefficients or standard errors. We will assess whether the age relationship needs a nonlinear term and compare observed and predicted concern rates across age groups and genders. A likelihood ratio test will compare models with and without the interaction. We will report odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p-values, and plot fitted probabilities across age for men and women at the same education level and country. These probability plots will help interpret the interaction.

\newpage

#### Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
#| label: pew-data
# Australia is excluded because it recorded age only in broad groups (see section 2)
pew <- read_sav("data/pew2025/Pew Research Center Global Attitudes Spring 2025 Dataset.sav") |>
  mutate(country = as_factor(country)) |>
  filter(country != "Australia") |>
  transmute(
    respondent_id = id,
    country       = fct_drop(country),
    ai_feeling = case_when(
      ai_cncexc == 1 ~ "More excited than concerned",
      ai_cncexc == 2 ~ "More concerned than excited",
      ai_cncexc == 3 ~ "Equally concerned and excited",
      ai_cncexc == 8 ~ "Don't know",
      ai_cncexc == 9 ~ "Refused"
    ),
    # Outcome: 1 = more concerned than excited, 0 = the other two answers
    concerned = case_when(ai_cncexc == 2 ~ 1, ai_cncexc %in% c(1, 3) ~ 0),
    gender    = case_when(gender == 1 ~ "Men", gender == 2 ~ "Women"),
    age_years = if_else(age < 98, as.numeric(age), NA),   # 98 and 99 mean no answer
    ai_awareness = case_when(
      ai_heard == 1 ~ "A lot",
      ai_heard == 2 ~ "A little",
      ai_heard == 3 ~ "Nothing at all"
    ) |> factor(levels = c("A lot", "A little", "Nothing at all"))
  )

# People who answered the AI question
pew_answered <- filter(pew, !is.na(concerned))

# Numbers quoted in the text
feel_pct   <- round(100 * prop.table(table(pew$ai_feeling)))
by_country <- pew_answered |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(share = mean(concerned)) |>
  arrange(share)
by_age_gender <- pew_answered |>
  filter(!is.na(gender), !is.na(age_years)) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age_years, c(17, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, Inf),
                         labels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70+"))) |>
  group_by(age_group, gender) |>
  summarise(share = mean(concerned), .groups = "drop")
gap <- pivot_wider(by_age_gender, names_from = gender, values_from = share)

glimpse(pew)
```

The data have `r comma(nrow(pew))` adults in `r n_distinct(pew$country)` countries, one per row. `r comma(sum(is.na(pew$concerned)))` people (`r percent(mean(is.na(pew$concerned)), accuracy = 1)`) answered "don't know" or refused the AI question; dropping them leaves `r comma(nrow(pew_answered))`. Of those, `r sum(is.na(pew_answered$gender))` are missing gender, `r sum(is.na(pew_answered$age_years))` age and `r sum(is.na(pew_answered$ai_awareness))` AI awareness. There are `r comma(sum(pew_answered$gender == "Women", na.rm = TRUE))` women and `r comma(sum(pew_answered$gender == "Men", na.rm = TRUE))` men, and the median age is `r median(pew_answered$age_years, na.rm = TRUE)` years. All summaries are unweighted.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pew-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Answers to \"How does the increased use of artificial intelligence in daily life make you feel?\", all 23 countries together."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 1.5
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(pew, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(ai_feeling)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6", width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Respondents", y = NULL)
```

The most common answer is equally concerned and excited (`r feel_pct[["Equally concerned and excited"]]`%), followed by more concerned than excited (`r feel_pct[["More concerned than excited"]]`%) and more excited than concerned (`r feel_pct[["More excited than concerned"]]`%) (@fig-pew-outcome). We will model a yes/no outcome: more concerned than excited, against the other two answers. "Don't know" and refusals are treated as missing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pew-interaction
#| fig-cap: "Share of respondents who are more concerned than excited about AI, by age group and gender, all 23 countries together."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(by_age_gender, aes(age_group, share, colour = gender, group = gender)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Women" = "#6250d6", "Men" = "#eb6834"), name = "Gender") +
  labs(x = "Age group (years)", y = "More concerned than excited about AI")
```

Concern rises steadily with age for both genders: from `r percent(gap$Men[1], accuracy = 1)` to `r percent(gap$Men[nrow(gap)], accuracy = 1)` for men and from `r percent(gap$Women[1], accuracy = 1)` to `r percent(gap$Women[nrow(gap)], accuracy = 1)` for women (@fig-pew-interaction). Women are more concerned in every age group, and the gap is `r round(100 * (gap$Women[1] - gap$Men[1]))` points in the youngest group and `r round(100 * (gap$Women[nrow(gap)] - gap$Men[nrow(gap)]))` points in the oldest. The steady rise supports using age in years in the model. This figure combines all countries, so the model will check whether the gender gap changes with age after adjusting for country.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pew-country
#| fig-cap: "Share of respondents who are more concerned than excited about AI, by country."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(by_country, aes(share, fct_reorder(country, share))) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "More concerned than excited about AI", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6.5))
```

Countries differ a lot: the share concerned runs from `r percent(by_country$share[1], accuracy = 1)` in `r by_country$country[1]` to `r percent(by_country$share[nrow(by_country)], accuracy = 1)` in `r by_country$country[nrow(by_country)]` (@fig-pew-country). The model will include country as a covariate.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pew-table1
#| tbl-cap: "Characteristics of men and women who answered the AI question, Pew Global Attitudes Spring 2025 (23 countries)."
pew_answered |>
  filter(!is.na(gender)) |>
  select(gender, concerned, age_years, ai_awareness, country) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = gender,
    missing_text = "Not reported",
    label = list(
      concerned    ~ "More concerned than excited about AI",
      age_years    ~ "Age (years)",
      ai_awareness ~ "Heard or read about AI",
      country      ~ "Country"
    )
  ) |>
  as_gt() |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::px(11), data_row.padding = gt::px(0))
```

The sample has more men than women, and the balance differs by country (@tbl-pew-table1). Men are also more likely to have heard a lot about AI. Education is not shown because it is recorded with different categories in each country; it will be harmonised into lower and higher education as described in section 3.3 before modelling.

## Team Charter

1.  When will you meet as a team to work on the project components? Will these meetings be held in person or virtually?

We will meet once a week, either in person or virtually, depending on everyone's schedules. We will use these meetings to plan tasks, review progress, and make decisions together. Between meetings, each member works on their assigned sections and pushes updates to our shared GitHub repository.

2.  What is your group policy on missing team meetings (e.g., how much advance notice should be provided)?

Members who cannot attend a meeting should let the team know at least 24 hours in advance, or as soon as possible in an emergency. The member who missed the meeting is responsible for catching up on what was discussed and completing their assigned tasks.

3.  How will your team communicate (email, Slack, text messages)? What is your policy on appropriate response time (within a certain number of hours? Nights/weekends?)?

We will communicate through our WhatsApp group chat for quick updates and questions, and use GitHub to share code and files. Whenever someone pushes changes to the repository, they will post a short message in the group chat so everyone can pull the latest version. We expect members to respond within 24 hours on weekdays. On nights and weekends, responses may take longer unless the matter is urgent.
